problem_text:
Назовём множество клеток \(M\) квадрата \(n\times n\) допустимым, если:

- никакие две клетки из \(M\) не смежны по ребру;
- после удаления всех клеток \(M\) каждая оставшаяся клетка имеет хотя бы одного соседа по ребру среди оставшихся клеток.

Пусть \(X_n\) — максимальный размер допустимого множества в квадрате \(n\times n\). Найдите
\[
\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{X_n}{n^2}.
\]

problem.title: Клетки
problem.statement:
Назовём множество клеток \(M\) квадрата \(n\times n\) допустимым, если:

- никакие две клетки из \(M\) не смежны по ребру;
- после удаления всех клеток \(M\) каждая оставшаяся клетка имеет хотя бы одного соседа по ребру среди оставшихся клеток.

Пусть \(X_n\) — максимальный размер допустимого множества в квадрате \(n\times n\). Найдите
\[
\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{X_n}{n^2}.
\]
problem.solution:
**Оценка.** Пусть \(M\) — допустимое множество, а \(R=V\setminus M\) — множество оставшихся клеток, где \(V\) — множество всех клеток квадрата \(n\times n\). Условия задачи означают, что:

- \(M\) независимо: никакие две клетки из \(M\) не смежны по ребру;
- каждая клетка из \(R\) имеет хотя бы одного соседа по ребру в \(R\), то есть \(R\) не содержит изолированных клеток.

Покажем, что каждая связная компонента \(R\), не касающаяся границы квадрата, содержит не менее \(5\) клеток. Предположим, что некоторая связная компонента \(C\subseteq R\) не касается границы и содержит не более \(4\) клеток. Рассмотрим все, с точностью до поворота и симметрии, связные фигуры, состоящие из \(1,2,3\) или \(4\) клеток:

![Связные фигуры из не более чем четырёх клеток](assets/task_05_small_components.png)

- \(1\) клетка. Единственная клетка компоненты не имеет соседей в \(R\), что противоречит второму условию.
- \(2,3\) или \(4\) клетки. У любой такой фигуры, не касающейся границы, найдётся сторона длины \(2\) на её границе — то есть два соседних ребра, смежных с двумя различными клетками из \(M\). Но тогда эти две клетки из \(M\) смежны друг с другом, что противоречит независимости \(M\).

Таким образом, ни одна из связных фигур из не более чем \(4\) клеток не может быть компонентой \(R\), не касающейся границы.

Рассмотрим граф соседств в решётке \(n\times n\), в нём
\[
2n(n-1)=2n^2+o(n^2)
\]
рёбер, и все дальнейшие рассуждения будут с точностью до \(o(n^2)\), что при делении на \(n^2\) в пределе даст нулевой вклад.

Пусть
\[
\alpha=\frac{|M|}{n^2}.
\]
Каждая клетка из \(M\) имеет ровно \(4\) соседей, и все они лежат в \(R\); кроме того, различные клетки из \(M\) не имеют общих соседей, так как \(M\) независимо. Следовательно, число рёбер между \(M\) и \(R\) равно в точности \(4\alpha n^2\).

С другой стороны, каждая связная компонента \(R\) из \(k\ge5\) клеток содержит не менее \(k-1\) рёбер, как связный граф. Отношение числа рёбер к числу клеток в такой компоненте не менее
\[
\frac{k-1}{k}\ge\frac45,
\]
откуда суммарное число рёбер внутри \(R\) не меньше
\[
\frac45(1-\alpha)n^2.
\]
Рёбра между \(M\) и \(R\) и рёбра внутри \(R\) попарно не пересекаются, и все они являются рёбрами решётки, поэтому
\[
4\alpha n^2+\frac45(1-\alpha)n^2\le2n^2+o(n^2).
\]
Раскрывая скобки и упрощая, получаем
\[
\alpha\le\frac38+o(1).
\]
То есть
\[
\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{X_n}{n^2}\le\frac38.
\]

**Пример.** Разобьём квадрат на области вертикальными и горизонтальными линиями с шагом \(4\). Получатся квадраты \(4\times4\), у границы могут получиться прямоугольники меньшего размера. Все внутренние области, не касающиеся границы, обязательно являются квадратами \(4\times4\). В каждую из них отметим по \(6\) клеток, как на картинке:

![Периодическая конструкция в квадратах 4 на 4](assets/task_05_pattern.png)

Поскольку объединение внутренних квадратов занимает \(n^2-o(n^2)\) клеток, а в каждом из них отмечена доля \(\frac38\) клеток, всего отмечена доля \(\frac38-o(1)\). То есть
\[
\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{X_n}{n^2}\ge\frac38.
\]

results.answer:
### Setup and notation.
Let \( G \) denote the \( n \times n \) grid graph (with the usual edge-adjacencies between cells). A set \( M \) is admissible precisely when \( M \) is an independent set in \( G \), and writing \( S := V(G) \setminus M \), the induced subgraph \( G\bigl[S\bigr] \) has minimum degree at least 1. (Equivalently, \( S \) is a vertex cover inducing no isolated vertices.) Thus \( X_n \) is the maximum size of an independent set whose complement induces minimum degree at least 1. We work throughout with the natural bipartition of \( G \) into black and white cells (according to the parity of \( i+j \)).

### The upper bound.
Write \( E_S \) for the number of edges in \( G\bigl[S\bigr] \), and let \( r := \frac{E_S}{\bigl|S\bigr|} \) (when \( S \neq \emptyset \)). Since \( \delta\bigl(G\bigl[S\bigr]\bigr) \geqslant 1 \), necessarily \( r \geqslant \frac12 \). A routine double-counting of edge endpoints, up to the usual \( O\bigl(n\bigr) \) discrepancies arising from the boundary of the grid (where degrees are strictly less than 4), yields the approximate relations \( 4\bigl|M\bigr| \approx e\bigl(M,\, S\bigr) \approx 4\bigl|S\bigr| - 2 E_S \). Rearranging, \( \frac{\bigl|M\bigr|}{n^2} \leqslant f\bigl(r\bigr) + o\bigl(1\bigr) \), where \( f\bigl(r\bigr) := \frac{1 - \frac12 r}{2 - \frac12 r} \). The function \( f \) is strictly decreasing for \( r \geqslant \frac12 \), with \( f\bigl(\frac12\bigr) = \frac37 \).

To upgrade this, we analyse the possible components of \( G\bigl[S\bigr] \). First, \( G\bigl[S\bigr] \) can have no component of size 2. Indeed, an isolated edge (domino) in the interior has each endpoint of induced degree 1, whence each of its three outer neighbours is forced into \( M \); but the two cells immediately “above” (or “below”) this domino are then adjacent elements of \( M \), contradicting independence of \( M \). The same local forcing rules out every component of size 3 (necessarily an induced path, whether straight or bent) and every component of size 4 (the possible induced trees being the path-tetrominoes \( \mathrm{I} \), \( \mathrm{L} \), \( \mathrm{S} \), and the branched tree \( \mathrm{T} \), together with the 4-cycle). In each case, the cells forced into \( M \) by the degree prescription in \( G\bigl[S\bigr] \) include at least one adjacent pair.

Thus every component of \( G\bigl[S\bigr] \) has size at least 5. Writing \( c \) for the number of components, we have \( E_S \geqslant \bigl|S\bigr| - c \) (since each component is connected), while \( c \leqslant \frac{\bigl|S\bigr|}{5} \), whence \( r \geqslant \frac45 \). (Boundary effects and components of size \( O\bigl(1\bigr) \) near the frontier of the grid contribute only \( O\bigl(n\bigr) \), so do not affect the limiting density.) Since \( f \) is decreasing we conclude \( \frac{\bigl|M\bigr|}{n^2} \leqslant f\bigl(\frac45\bigr) + o\bigl(1\bigr) = \frac38 + o\bigl(1\bigr) \), or more precisely \( X_n \leqslant \frac38 n^2 + O\bigl(n\bigr) \).

### The matching lower bound.
It remains to exhibit admissible sets achieving density \( \frac38 \). To this end, fix the black/white colouring of the infinite grid as above, and let \( D \) be the set of all black cells of the form \( \bigl(4k,\, 4m\bigr) \) or \( \bigl(4k+2,\, 4m+2\bigr) \). Each cell of \( D \) is adjacent to four white cells, and these 4-neighbourhoods are pairwise disjoint and exhaust all white cells. Let \( S \) comprise all white cells together with \( D \), and let \( M \) comprise the remaining black cells. Then \( M \) is independent (as a subset of the black cells). The induced subgraph \( G\bigl[S\bigr] \) consists precisely of disjoint copies of the star \( K_{1,4} \) (each centred at an element of \( D \)), whence in particular \( \delta\bigl(G\bigl[S\bigr]\bigr) \geqslant 1 \). The construction is 4-periodic, with precisely 2 elements of \( D \) and 6 elements of \( M \) in each \( 4 \times 4 \) block, so that the density of \( M \) is exactly \( \frac38 \). Restricting to large finite \( n \times n \) grids (and discarding at most an \( O\bigl(n\bigr) \) frontier error) therefore yields admissible sets with \( \bigl|M\bigr| \geqslant \frac38 n^2 - O\bigl(n\bigr) \), whence \( X_n \geqslant \frac38 n^2 - O\bigl(n\bigr) \).

### Conclusion.
Combining the matching upper and lower estimates, we deduce that the limit exists and equals \( \frac38 \).

Let \( G \) denote the \( n \times n \) grid graph (with the usual edge-adjacencies between cells). A set \( M \) is admissible precisely when \( M \) is an independent set in \( G \), and writing \( S := V(G) \setminus M \), the induced subgraph \( G\bigl[S\bigr] \) has minimum degree at least 1. (Equivalently, \( S \) is a vertex cover inducing no isolated vertices.) Thus \( X_n \) is the maximum size of an independent set whose complement induces minimum degree at least 1. We work throughout with the natural bipartition of \( G \) into black and white cells (according to the parity of \( i+j \)).

### The upper bound.
Write \( E_S \) for the number of edges in \( G\bigl[S\bigr] \), and let \( r := \frac{E_S}{\bigl|S\bigr|} \) (when \( S \neq \emptyset \)). Since \( \delta\bigl(G\bigl[S\bigr]\bigr) \geqslant 1 \), necessarily \( r \geqslant \frac12 \). A routine double-counting of edge endpoints, up to the usual \( O\bigl(n\bigr) \) discrepancies arising from the boundary of the grid (where degrees are strictly less than 4), yields the approximate relations \( 4\bigl|M\bigr| \approx e\bigl(M,\, S\bigr) \approx 4\bigl|S\bigr| - 2 E_S \). Rearranging, \( \frac{\bigl|M\bigr|}{n^2} \leqslant f\bigl(r\bigr) + o\bigl(1\bigr) \), where \( f\bigl(r\bigr) := \frac{1 - \frac12 r}{2 - \frac12 r} \). The function \( f \) is strictly decreasing for \( r \geqslant \frac12 \), with \( f\bigl(\frac12\bigr) = \frac37 \).

To upgrade this, we analyse the possible components of \( G\bigl[S\bigr] \). First, \( G\bigl[S\bigr] \) can have no component of size 2. Indeed, an isolated edge (domino) in the interior has each endpoint of induced degree 1, whence each of its three outer neighbours is forced into \( M \); but the two cells immediately “above” (or “below”) this domino are then adjacent elements of \( M \), contradicting independence of \( M \). The same local forcing rules out every component of size 3 (necessarily an induced path, whether straight or bent) and every component of size 4 (the possible induced trees being the path-tetrominoes \( \mathrm{I} \), \( \mathrm{L} \), \( \mathrm{S} \), and the branched tree \( \mathrm{T} \), together with the 4-cycle). In each case, the cells forced into \( M \) by the degree prescription in \( G\bigl[S\bigr] \) include at least one adjacent pair.

Thus every component of \( G\bigl[S\bigr] \) has size at least 5. Writing \( c \) for the number of components, we have \( E_S \geqslant \bigl|S\bigr| - c \) (since each component is connected), while \( c \leqslant \frac{\bigl|S\bigr|}{5} \), whence \( r \geqslant \frac45 \). (Boundary effects and components of size \( O\bigl(1\bigr) \) near the frontier of the grid contribute only \( O\bigl(n\bigr) \), so do not affect the limiting density.) Since \( f \) is decreasing we conclude \( \frac{\bigl|M\bigr|}{n^2} \leqslant f\bigl(\frac45\bigr) + o\bigl(1\bigr) = \frac38 + o\bigl(1\bigr) \), or more precisely \( X_n \leqslant \frac38 n^2 + O\bigl(n\bigr) \).

It remains to exhibit admissible sets achieving density \( \frac38 \). Each cell of \( D \) is adjacent to four white cells, and these 4-neighbourhoods are pairwise disjoint and exhaust all white cells. Let \( S \) comprise all white cells together with \( D \), and let \( M \) comprise the remaining black cells. Then \( M \) is independent (as a subset of the black cells). The induced subgraph \( G\bigl[S\bigr] \) consists precisely of disjoint copies of the star \( K_{1,4} \) (each centred at an element of \( D \)), whence in particular \( \delta\bigl(G\bigl[S\bigr]\bigr) \geqslant 1 \). The construction is 4-periodic, with precisely 2 elements of \( D \) and 6 elements of \( M \) in each \( 4 \times 4 \) block, so that the density of \( M \) is exactly \( \frac38 \). ### Conclusion.
Combining the matching upper and lower estimates, we deduce that the limit exists and equals \( \frac38 \).

### Setup and notation.
Let \( G \) denote the \( n \times n \) grid graph (with the usual edge-adjacencies between cells). A set \( M \) is admissible precisely when \( M \) is an independent set in \( G \), and writing \( S := V(G) \setminus M \), the induced subgraph \( G\bigl[S\bigr] \) has minimum degree at least 1. (Equivalently, \( S \) is a vertex cover inducing no isolated vertices.) Thus \( X_n \) is the maximum size of an independent set whose complement induces minimum degree at least 1. We work throughout with the natural bipartition of \( G \) into black and white cells (according to the parity of \( i+j \)).

### The upper bound.
Write \( E_S \) for the number of edges in \( G\bigl[S\bigr] \), and let \( r := \frac{E_S}{\bigl|S\bigr|} \) (when \( S \neq \emptyset \)). Since \( \delta\bigl(G\bigl[S\bigr]\bigr) \geqslant 1 \), necessarily \( r \geqslant \frac12 \). A routine double-counting of edge endpoints, up to the usual \( O\bigl(n\bigr) \) discrepancies arising from the boundary of the grid (where degrees are strictly less than 4), yields the approximate relations \( 4\bigl|M\bigr| \approx e\bigl(M,\, S\bigr) \approx 4\bigl|S\bigr| - 2 E_S \). Rearranging, \( \frac{\bigl|M\bigr|}{n^2} \leqslant f\bigl(r\bigr) + o\bigl(1\bigr) \), where \( f\bigl(r\bigr) := \frac{1 - \frac12 r}{2 - \frac12 r} \). The function \( f \) is strictly decreasing for \( r \geqslant \frac12 \), with \( f\bigl(\frac12\bigr) = \frac37 \).

To upgrade this, we analyse the possible components of \( G\bigl[S\bigr] \). First, \( G\bigl[S\bigr] \) can have no component of size 2. Indeed, an isolated edge (domino) in the interior has each endpoint of induced degree 1, whence each of its three outer neighbours is forced into \( M \); but the two cells immediately “above” (or “below”) this domino are then adjacent elements of \( M \), contradicting independence of \( M \). The same local forcing rules out every component of size 3 (necessarily an induced path, whether straight or bent) and every component of size 4 (the possible induced trees being the path-tetrominoes \( \mathrm{I} \), \( \mathrm{L} \), \( \mathrm{S} \), and the branched tree \( \mathrm{T} \), together with the 4-cycle). In each case, the cells forced into \( M \) by the degree prescription in \( G\bigl[S\bigr] \) include at least one adjacent pair.

Thus every component of \( G\bigl[S\bigr] \) has size at least 5. Writing \( c \) for the number of components, we have \( E_S \geqslant \bigl|S\bigr| - c \) (since each component is connected), while \( c \leqslant \frac{\bigl|S\bigr|}{5} \), whence \( r \geqslant \frac45 \). (Boundary effects and components of size \( O\bigl(1\bigr) \) near the frontier of the grid contribute only \( O\bigl(n\bigr) \), so do not affect the limiting density.) Since \( f \) is decreasing we conclude \( \frac{\bigl|M\bigr|}{n^2} \leqslant f\bigl(\frac45\bigr) + o\bigl(1\bigr) = \frac38 + o\bigl(1\bigr) \), or more precisely \( X_n \leqslant \frac38 n^2 + O\bigl(n\bigr) \).

### The matching lower bound.
It remains to exhibit admissible sets achieving density \( \frac38 \). To this end, fix the black/white colouring of the infinite grid as above, and let \( D \) be the set of all black cells of the form \( \bigl(4k,\, 4m\bigr) \) or \( \bigl(4k+2,\, 4m+2\bigr) \). Each cell of \( D \) is adjacent to four white cells, and these 4-neighbourhoods are pairwise disjoint and exhaust all white cells. Let \( S \) comprise all white cells together with \( D \), and let \( M \) comprise the remaining black cells. Then \( M \) is independent (as a subset of the black cells). The induced subgraph \( G\bigl[S\bigr] \) consists precisely of disjoint copies of the star \( K_{1,4} \) (each centred at an element of \( D \)), whence in particular \( \delta\bigl(G\bigl[S\bigr]\bigr) \geqslant 1 \). The construction is 4-periodic, with precisely 2 elements of \( D \) and 6 elements of \( M \) in each \( 4 \times 4 \) block, so that the density of \( M \) is exactly \( \frac38 \). Restricting to large finite \( n \times n \) grids (and discarding at most an \( O\bigl(n\bigr) \) frontier error) therefore yields admissible sets with \( \bigl|M\bigr| \geqslant \frac38 n^2 - O\bigl(n\bigr) \), whence \( X_n \geqslant \frac38 n^2 - O\bigl(n\bigr) \).

### Conclusion.
Combining the matching upper and lower estimates, we deduce that the limit exists and equals \( \frac38 \).
